subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: When asked to identify the AUDIENCE of a text titled "A Beginner's Guide to Filing Your First Tax Return," the clearest clue is that it targets:
options: People doing this task for the first time
questions.explain: The words "beginner" and "first" signal an audience new to the task.

questions.q: Which is the clearest sign of the intended AUDIENCE in "Top tips for surviving your first term at uni"?
options: It is aimed at retired people
Casual language and the reference to "uni" suggest young/new students
questions.explain: Informal tone and student-focused content signal a young, new-undergraduate audience.

questions.q: When comparing two non-fiction texts, an exam asks about their "viewpoints and methods." "Methods" mainly means:
options: The techniques each writer uses to put their view across
questions.explain: "Methods" refers to the language and structural techniques used to convey the viewpoint.

questions.q: An extract opens with a long, calm description of a sunny garden, then a single line: "Then the screaming began." What is the structural effect of this shift?
options: It signals the end of the story
It creates a jarring contrast that shocks the reader
It tells us the setting is unimportant
questions.explain: The sudden shift from calm to violence creates contrast and shock, a deliberate structural effect.

questions.q: Addressing the reader as "you" in a persuasive article is known as:
questions.explain: Speaking straight to the reader using "you" is direct address.

questions.q: A writer describes a character who "forced a thin smile and changed the subject quickly." What can you most reasonably INFER?
options: The character is uncomfortable and wants to avoid the topic
The character has just woken up
The character is about to tell a long story
The character is feeling genuinely cheerful
questions.explain: A forced smile and a quick subject-change imply discomfort and avoidance rather than the explicit emotion of happiness.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a writer SHOWING rather than TELLING emotion?
options: "She bit her nails and glanced at the door again and again."
questions.explain: Describing actions (nail-biting, glancing) lets the reader infer nervousness, which is "showing."

questions.q: A dove is used throughout a text to represent peace. Using an object to stand for an idea is:
questions.explain: An object standing for a larger idea (a dove for peace) is symbolism.

questions.q: "Do we really want our children breathing this filthy air?" Which technique is this?
questions.explain: It is a question asked for effect, not for an answer: a rhetorical question.

questions.q: Which choice best describes the ATMOSPHERE in "Sunlight spilled across the kitchen and the kettle hummed a cheerful tune"?
questions.explain: Sunlight, a humming kettle and a "cheerful" tune build a warm, comforting atmosphere.

questions.q: Early in a story, a character nervously eyes a loaded gun on the wall. Hinting at a later event is:
questions.explain: Planting an early hint of something to come is foreshadowing.

questions.q: To "zoom in" on the quotation "her hands trembled like leaves in a storm," the strongest analytical move is to:
options: Say it is a nice description
Comment on the simile and what the comparison suggests about her
questions.explain: Zooming in means analysing the chosen technique (a simile) and the specific impression it gives.

questions.q: Which feature most clearly signals that a text's purpose is to INFORM rather than persuade?
options: Commands telling the reader what to do
Neutral, factual statements presented in a balanced way
questions.explain: A neutral, balanced presentation of facts is characteristic of writing that informs.

questions.q: "Over 90% of teachers agree that homework helps." Which persuasive device is used here?
questions.explain: A figure or percentage used to support a point is a statistic.

questions.q: "The town had not changed, yet nothing felt the same to him now." This sentence mainly invites the reader to focus on:
options: How the character himself has changed inside
questions.explain: The contrast between an unchanged town and altered feeling points to internal change in the character.

questions.q: When an extract suddenly shifts focus from a wide view of a crowd to one trembling child, this structural technique:
options: Narrows the focus to direct the reader's attention
Changes the narrator to second person
questions.explain: Moving from the general to a single detail is a deliberate narrowing of focus that guides reader attention.

questions.q: A newspaper report only quotes critics of a policy and ignores its supporters. This shows:
questions.explain: Presenting one side while leaving out the other is bias.

questions.q: A travel article says "You will love every breathtaking moment of this paradise." What is its main PURPOSE?
options: To persuade the reader to visit
questions.explain: Positive, emotive language directed at "you" is designed to persuade the reader to go.

questions.q: "She laughed, but her eyes stayed cold." The contrast in this sentence most strongly suggests her laughter is:
options: Insincere or hiding her true feelings
questions.explain: Warm laughter set against cold eyes implies the laughter is false and conceals real feeling.

questions.q: In a story, a storm rages whenever the hero is angry. The weather reflecting emotion is:
questions.explain: Using weather/nature to mirror a character's mood is pathetic fallacy.

questions.q: Identifying a writer's VIEWPOINT means working out:
options: Their attitude or opinion towards the subject
questions.explain: Viewpoint is the writer's stance or attitude on the topic.

questions.q: "The wind whispered through the trees." Which technique is this?
questions.explain: Giving the wind the human ability to "whisper" is personification.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500) syllabus; Paper 1 Reading
